title: Architecture & Standards: Unified Guidelines and ADRs (API, Coding, Infra, Model Serving, Observability, Performance)
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

Purpose: This page consolidates Redwood Inference’s authoritative architecture and standards for API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. It also records key architecture decision records (ADRs) that drive long-lived constraints in the platform. Teams should use these guidelines when designing services, reviewing PRs, and writing runbooks.

Scope: applies to all public and internal services that serve inference traffic or participate in inference data pipelines (hosted API, dedicated, private).

1) API Standards

Introduction
- Goal: predictable, REST/JSON and gRPC APIs with consistent observability, versioning, and error semantics.
- Target consumers: external customers (hosted API), internal services, and sync/async worker systems.

Guidelines
- API versions: use semver-like path versioning (/v1/, /v2/) for public endpoints. Backwards-incompatible changes require a new major version and an ADR.
- Transport: HTTP/1.1 + TLS1.2+ for public endpoints; internal services may use HTTP/2 or gRPC.
- Authentication: OAuth2 bearer tokens for hosted API; mTLS for private deployments by default.
- Request/response shape: JSON objects; prefer explicit fields over arbitrary blobs. Use top-level envelope for metadata: {"request_id":"", "client_id":"", "payload":{...}}.
- Error model: standardize on problem-details JSON (RFC 7807). Required fields: type, title, status, detail, request_id. Map internal error codes into stable error types for customers.
- Pagination: cursor-based pagination for large lists; avoid page numbers for performance-sensitive endpoints.
- Rate limiting headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.
- Streaming: use chunked transfer or server-sent-events for model token streaming. Ensure each chunk is a valid JSON fragment per the streaming contract.

Example (generation request):
``
POST /v1/generate HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{
  "request_id": "r-12345",
  "client_id": "acme-frontend",
  "payload": {
    "model": "redwood-v1.1",
    "input": "Summarize the following text...",
    "max_tokens": 512
  }
}
```

API Review checklist (for API owners to answer in PR):
1. Is the endpoint backward compatible? If not, has an ADR been opened?
2. Are schemas validated and documented with examples?
3. Are SLO and quota implications reviewed?
4. Are observability hooks (tracing/span names, metrics, logs) included?
5. Has authentication and authorization been verified?

2) Coding Standards

Goals: maintainable, testable, and performance-sensitive code across runtime and control-plane services.

General rules
- Languages in use: Go for control plane services, Rust/C++ for serving runtime hot paths, Python for infra automation and eval tooling.
- Formatting and linting: adopt gofmt/golangci-lint, rustfmt/clippy, and black/ruff for Python. Fail CI on new lint errors.
- Typing: prefer strong typing; use linters to catch unsafe casts.
- Tests: unit tests for logic, integration tests for cross-service contracts; end-to-end smoke tests for deployment. Coverage gates: >= 80% for new modules touching billing/security logic; recommended 60% elsewhere.
- PR size: keep under 400 lines for reviewability. Use ADR for exceptions.

Concurrency & performance practices
- Avoid unbounded goroutines/tasks for request handling — use worker pools or rate-limited queues.
- Prefer asynchronous IO where appropriate; annotate blocking syscalls in code comments.
- Hot path instrumentation: annotate functions in serving runtime that are on token-generation path; minimize allocations and dynamic dispatch.

Secrets and config
- Never store plaintext secrets in repo. Use Secrets Manager (internal KMS wrapper). CI must inject secrets at runtime only.

3) Infrastructure Standards

Ownership: infra standards are owned by eng-infra with platform stewardship by eng-platform.

Networking & security
- VPCs per environment (prod/staging/dev). Prod VPCs segmented by customer tier.
- Private deployments: default to customer-managed VPC peering + dedicated routing. mTLS and KMS-backed encryption in transit and at rest.
- Firewall rules: deny-by-default; expose only documented ports.

Compute and capacity
- Serving runtime instances are GPU-backed machine images with preinstalled runtime artifacts. Image versions are mapped to model versions via artifact registry tags.
- Autoscaling: use target CPU/GPU utilization with cooldown windows. Baseline scaling policies: min=2, target_util=70%, cooldown=5m for critical pools.

IaC and provisioning
- Terraform modules standard for core infra. Module schema table:
| Module | Purpose | Required inputs | Outputs/Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| network | VPC, subnets, route tables | region, cidr_block, environment | network_id / eng-infra |
| gpu_pool | GPU autoscaling pools | instance_type, min_size, max_size | pool_id / eng-sre |
| kms | Key management | key_policy | key_arn / security |

Deployment policy
1. All infra changes require a plan output and peer review.
2. Apply in staging, run smoke tests, verify SLOs, then schedule prod rollout.
3. Use blue/green for control-plane and canary for serving runtime when supported.

4) Model-serving Standards

Objective: serve models with predictable latency, cost, and correctness.

Model packaging and versioning
- Model artifact manifest (YAML) required for every model with fields: model_name, version, framework, quantization_profile, expected_memory_gb, max_sequence_length, session_kv_cache_support (true/false).
- Example manifest snippet:
```
model_name: redwood-v1.1
version: 2026-01-10
framework: pytorch
quantization_profile: q4_0
expected_memory_gb: "42"
max_sequence_length: "2048"
session_kv_cache_support: "true"
```

Serving runtime requirements
- KV cache: support for prefix caching across requests with configurable TTL. Default TTL=300s.
- Batching: continuous batching with max batch size per-GPU driven by benchmarking profile. Batching profiles stored in config repo per model.
- Fallbacks: runtime must support automatic downgrade to CPU-compatible variant or smaller model when GPU capacity is exhausted.

SLOs and resource accounting
- Per-model SLOs: default p95 latency <= 350ms for small models (<= 10B tokens per request) and p95 <= 1s for large models; target throughput and token/sec budgets defined in model manifest.
- Cost attribution: track GPU-minutes, memory usage, and token counts per request. Billing pipeline ingests these metrics for downstream invoicing.

Model rollout checklist (numbered procedure)
1. Add model manifest and quantization profile to model registry.
2. Benchmark: run perf suite (see section "Benchmarking and perf suite") and record profile.
3. Stage deploy to dedicated pool with canary traffic (1% for 2h). Monitor latencies, error rates, and qualitative evals.
4. Gradually increase to 25%/50%/100% with pause windows and automated rollback on thresholds.

5) Observability Standards

Goals: fast detection of regressions, clear owner for each alert, and traceable request flows across control plane and runtime.

Tracing and logs
- Distributed tracing: use W3C trace-context. Span naming conventions: service.operation.resource (e.g., api.generate.request). Include model_name and model_version as span tags.
- Logs: structured JSON logs with keys: timestamp, level, service, env, request_id, trace_id, message, details. Redact PII.

Metrics and dashboards
- Metric naming: snake_case, hierarchical: <service>_<component>_<metric>. Examples: api_requests_total, runtime_token_generation_latency_ms, gpu_utilization_pct.
- Required metrics for any serving endpoint:
  - requests_total (by endpoint, model)
  - request_errors_total (by error_type)
  - request_latency_ms_p50/p95/p99
  - tokens_generated_total
  - gpu_minutes_consumed_total
- Dashboards: per-model and per-route dashboards with: latency heatmap, error rate, throughput, cost per 1k tokens.

Alerting
- Alert should answer: what, who, and next action. Use runbook links in alert text.
- Ownership: every alert must map to a single primary oncall team.
- Alert thresholds (examples):
  - P95 latency increase > 25% above baseline for 10m -> severity P2
  - Error rate > 1% for 5m -> severity P1
  - GPU pool free capacity < 10% -> severity P2

6) Performance Standards and Benchmarking

Benchmarking suite
- Centralized perf suite located in eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite. Includes microbenchmarks, end-to-end latency tests, and cost-per-token experiments.
- Bench rules: run benchmarks on identical machine images and record metadata: image_id, driver_version, kernel, cuda/cuDNN versions, model manifest used.

Performance targets
- Baseline SLOs (production):
  - Small models (<= 10B params): p95 <= 350ms, p99 <= 800ms
  - Medium models (10B-70B): p95 <= 750ms, p99 <= 2.5s
  - Large models (>70B): p95 <= 1.5s, p99 <= 4.0s
- Cost targets: cost per 1k tokens must be tracked and flagged if > 20% above modeled cost for 24h.

Regression testing
- Continuous perf regression detection: weekly benchmark runs compared to baseline. If a regression > 10% p95 is detected, create regression-YYYYMMDD ticket and notify owners.

7) ADRs (Architecture Decision Records)

Purpose: document trade-offs and stable decisions that impact multiple teams. ADR format: ID, Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives. ADRs are stored under architecture-and-standards/decision-records and referenced here.

Selected current ADRs (examples)
| ADR | Title | Status | Owner | Date | Summary |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ADR-2025-07 | Model quantization defaults | accepted | Research/Applied ML | 2025-07-21 | Default quantization profile for large open models set to q4_0 for production — reduces memory by ~60% with ~2-3% quality regression.
| ADR-2025-11 | API versioning strategy | accepted | Eng-API | 2025-11-03 | Use path-major-versioning (/vN/) with explicit deprecation windows and compatibility tests.
| ADR-2026-01 | Runtime kernel selection | accepted | Eng-Serving-Runtime | 2026-01-15 | Runtime will select kernels at model load time based on architecture and workload telemetry; dynamic swapping disabled during active sessions.

How to create an ADR
1. Draft ADR using ADR template in the repo.
2. Add to /confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records with initial status proposed.
3. Seek reviewers from affected teams; update and move to accepted/rejected.

8) Governance and Review Process

- Standards board: a rotating committee (architecture guild) meets biweekly to review high-impact proposals and ADRs. Membership includes representatives from eng-serving-runtime, eng-infra, eng-sre, research, and product.
- Exceptions: teams may request exceptions by filing an "architecture exception" doc and presenting to the standards board. Exceptions expire after 6 months unless renewed.
